sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Presents a conceptual cost estimating method for micropile projects. The method uses a 2004 baseline cost of approximately $300/linear meter as the average U.S. micropile price (post-decade of cost reduction), then applies project-specific adjustment factors from Table 10-4. Cost breakdown (Table 10-1): material 25-40%, equipment 20-30%, labor 25-60%, load testing <5%. The estimate method is similar to a conceptual engineering cost estimate: identifies highest-impact cost components without requiring specific bid quantities.
sections.body: The purpose of this chapter is to present an approach that may be used to develop a cost estimate for any micropile project. The cost estimate method described is similar to a conceptual cost estimate in engineering practice: sufficient detail is used to identify the cost components which may have the largest effect on total project cost, however specific bid quantities and potential bidding contractors are not necessarily known. The method requires that a baseline cost for micropiles be known. Over the past ten years (as of 2004), numerous micropile projects have been completed in the United States and typical micropile costs have decreased mostly due to experience gained by specialty micropile contractors and advances in micropile installation equipment. In 2004, a reasonable average price for micropiles is on the order of $300 per linear meter of micropile. The typical breakdown of micropile unit costs is: material 25-40%, equipment 20-30%, labor 25-60%, and load testing less than 5% (Table 10-1). Note that costs cited in this chapter are representative of 2004 conditions and should be adjusted for current market conditions.
key_points: Baseline cost (2004): ~$300/linear meter average U.S. micropile price
Cost breakdown (Table 10-1): material 25-40%, equipment 20-30%, labor 25-60%, testing <5%
Costs decreased over prior decade due to contractor experience and equipment advances
Method: apply project-specific adjustment factors to $300/m baseline
Costs cited are 2004 representative values — adjust for current market conditions

sections.applicability: Developing preliminary conceptual cost estimates for micropile projects before detailed design is complete.

sections.title: Factors That Influence Micropile Costs
sections.summary: Identifies four primary cost components and their 2004 representative values. Material costs (Tables 10-2, 10-3): steel casing $15-25/m (140mm), $35-45/m (178mm); rebar $20-26/m (57mm), $26-32/m (64mm); threading adds ~$60/m. Equipment costs have decreased with increased availability. Labor: 4-person crew installs 6-20 piles per day (15m piles); labor is 25-30% of cost in easy conditions, up to 60% in urban/difficult access. Load testing: typically <5% of project cost.
sections.body: Micropile costs are driven by four primary components: materials, equipment, labor, and load testing. Micropile Material Costs: The most commonly used steel casings have outside diameters of 140mm (5.5 in.), 178mm (7 in.), and 245mm (9-5/8 in.). Representative 2004 casing costs (without threads): 139.7mm = $15-25/m; 177.8mm = $35-45/m (Table 10-2). Threading adds significantly: for 140mm casing, threading one 1-m section costs approximately $60 (3 times the casing cost). The most common reinforcement bars have diameters of 57mm (2-1/4 in.) and 64mm (2-1/2 in.). Representative 2004 bar costs: 57mm = $20-26/m; 64mm = $26-32/m (Table 10-3). Equipment Costs: Overall equipment costs have decreased in recent years due to greater availability of drilling equipment specialized for micropile applications. Equipment typically represents 20-30% of the total micropile unit cost. Labor Costs: A typical micropile crew consists of four individuals: project superintendent, drilling operator, and two laborers. For relatively easy drilling conditions and low-to-moderate capacity micropiles, a typical crew may install up to 6 to 20 piles (15m maximum) per day. Labor comprises 25-30% of total cost in easy conditions with moderate productivity. In tight access areas and difficult drilling conditions, labor may increase to 30-45% of total cost. In extra labor-intensive projects and high-wage urban areas, labor may reach 60% of micropile costs. Load Testing Costs: Load testing costs depend on site access, load type, and whether reaction is provided by the ground. Load testing typically represents less than 5% of total project cost.
key_points: Casing costs (2004, no threads): 140mm = $15-25/m; 178mm = $35-45/m (Table 10-2)
Threading cost for 140mm casing ≈ $60/m — 3x the raw casing cost
Crew: 4 persons — superintendent, drill operator, 2 laborers
Productivity: 6-20 piles/day for easy drilling (15m piles max); decreases significantly in difficult conditions
Labor: 25-30% in easy access; up to 60% in urban/difficult access
Load testing: typically <5% of total project cost

sections.title: Micropile Cost Analysis
sections.summary: Cost analysis method applies project-specific adjustment factors from Table 10-4 to the $300/m baseline. Factors and ranges: physical/access conditions 0-100%, geology/ground conditions 0-50%, pile capacity -30 to +30%, pile lengths -25 to +25%, pile quantities -30 to +10%, testing requirements 0-15%, mobilization/demobilization 0-10%, continuous drilling -5 to 0%, union agreements 0-10%, overhead and profit -10 to +10%. Two sample problems: (1) bridge abutment with difficult geology = $555/m = $6,660/pile (12m); (2) seismic retrofit San Francisco = $300 × 1.10 = $330/m.
sections.body: An owner considering micropiles may use the average cost of $300 per linear meter with modifications from Table 10-4 to develop a preliminary cost estimate. Table 10-4 reflects the relative effect of project-specific factors on micropile construction costs based on contractor input. Cost adjustment factors and ranges include: physical and access conditions (very easy to very difficult): 0% to +100%; geology/ground conditions (very easy to very difficult): 0% to +50%; pile capacity (very low to very high): -30% to +30%; pile lengths (very short to very long): -25% to +25%; pile quantities (very small to very large): -30% to +10%; testing requirements (none to extensive): 0% to +15%; mobilization/demobilization: 0% to +10%; continuous drilling operations: -5% to 0%; union agreements: 0% to +10%; overhead and profit: -10% to +10%. Sample Problem 1 (Bridge Abutment Support): Easy access (+10%), difficult drilling due to cobbles/boulders (+30%), moderate pile capacity (+5%), moderate pile length (+5%), small quantity (+10%), verification + 2 proof tests (+10%), single mobilization (+5%), non-continuous setup (+0%), no union agreement (+0%), moderate risk project (+10%). Total adjustment = +85%. Cost = $300 × (1 + 85/100) = $555/linear meter. For 12m piles: $555 × 12 = $6,660 each. Sample Problem 2 (Seismic Retrofit): San Francisco viaduct, 360 micropiles at 20m average, total adjustment = +10%. Cost = $300 × 1.10 = $330/m.
key_points: Cost = $300/m baseline × (1 + sum of adjustment factors from Table 10-4)
Largest factors: access conditions (0-100%), geology (0-50%); pile quantity can reduce cost (-30%)
Sample Problem 1 (bridge abutment, difficult geology): $555/m = $6,660/pile at 12m
Sample Problem 2 (seismic retrofit, SF, 360 piles at 20m): $330/m (only +10% total adjustment)
Table 10-4 covers 10 adjustment factors based on contractor input data
Add separate pay items for difficult conditions (e.g., grout volume for karst terrain)

sections.title: Measurement and Payment for Micropiles
sections.summary: Defines standard payment units for micropile projects (Table 10-7). Mobilization/demobilization: lump sum. Preproduction test pile program: lump sum. Verification load test: per each. Proof load test: per each. Furnish and install production micropile (foundation support): per each. Furnish and install micropile (slope stabilization): per lineal meter of cap beam. Notes that additional pay items should be developed for difficult ground conditions such as karst (grout volume above theoretical minimum).
sections.body: Measurement and payment for micropile projects should use the standard payment units provided in Table 10-7. Mobilization/demobilization is paid on a lump-sum basis. The preproduction test pile program is paid as a lump sum. Individual verification load tests and proof load tests are paid per each. Production micropiles for foundation support are paid on a per-each (per pile) basis. Micropiles for slope stabilization are paid on a per lineal meter of cap beam basis, since the number of piles per unit length of cap beam varies based on required spacing. Additional pay items should be developed for projects involving difficult ground conditions in which specific problems may be anticipated during the bid period. For example, where micropiles are to be installed in karstic regions, a pay item for grout volume above some minimum volume (typically two times the theoretical volume) should be included in the specifications. Specifications should require that where grout volumes exceed twice the theoretical volume, the contractor document the additional grout and be compensated for it.
key_points: Mobilization/demobilization: lump sum
Preproduction test pile program: lump sum
Verification and proof load tests: per each
Foundation support micropiles: per each (per pile)
Slope stabilization micropiles: per lineal meter of cap beam (variable piles per meter)
Karst terrain: include pay item for grout volume above 2x theoretical; document and compensate excess
tables: Table 10-7: Micropile Measurement and Payment Units
sections.applicability: Establishing contract pay items and measurement methods for micropile projects.
